title: embed.FS: shipping static assets in the binary
summary: A //go:embed directive makes the compiler copy files into the binary as a string, a []byte or a read-only embed.FS. Because embed.FS is an fs.FS, templates and HTTP file servers use it directly: one file to deploy.

examples.title: string, embed.FS, the hidden-file rule and all:

annotations.note: The directive sits directly above a package-level variable. For a string or []byte it must match exactly one file, and the file's content becomes the variable's value at compile time.

Naming a directory embeds its whole subtree except names that start with . or _, so editor backups and .env files stay out. The all: prefix turns that filter off, which is how secrets end up in a binary.
The binary doesn't read version.txt at run time; the compiler already did. Changing the file changes nothing until the next go build.
Embedded names are slash-separated, relative to the package directory, and include the directory you named: static/app.css, not app.css.
A file excluded by the pattern simply isn't there: Open returns an error wrapping fs.ErrNotExist.

examples.title: ParseFS and FileServerFS on embedded files, a MapFS in tests

annotations.note: Two variables, two patterns. templates/*.tmpl matches files only; a * pattern would also match .hidden files at that level, unlike a bare directory name.
The handler depends on fs.FS, the interface, so the embedding decision stays in main. This is what lets the last request run against an in-memory test file system.
http.FileServerFS (Go 1.22) serves any fs.FS. StripPrefix removes /static/ from the URL so the remaining path matches names in the sub-tree.
ParseFS takes path.Match patterns over the FS. fs.Sub returns the static directory as its own FS, so names lose the static/ prefix.
r.PathValue returns the decoded name, Ayşe, and html/template escapes it for HTML: the <script> attempt arrives as text.
_draft.html is on disk next to the source but was never embedded, so the file server answers 404.
fstest.MapFS is a map from names to files that satisfies fs.FS, so a test can swap the assets without touching disk or the build.

use_cases: Single-binary deployment: HTML templates, CSS, JS and a built SPA inside one executable (or one FROM scratch image)
SQL migrations embedded next to the code that runs them
Default config files, license texts, test fixtures and seed data
strengths: No path resolution at run time: the binary works from any working directory, unlike reading ./templates relative to where the process started
Plugs into everything that takes an fs.FS: html/template.ParseFS, http.FileServerFS, fs.WalkDir, migration tools

Built into the go command, no bundler, resource compiler or build step, unlike Java resources (which need the JAR packaging) or Node, which needs a bundler or its experimental single-executable feature
weaknesses: Every change needs a rebuild; in development you usually want os.DirFS for live edits
Read-only, and files carry no modification time, so http.FileServer can't send Last-Modified or answer 304 on its own
The binary grows by the size of the files, and patterns can't reach outside the package directory (no .., no parent folders)

pitfalls.title: all: embeds secrets
pitfalls.detail: all:static includes .env, .git leftovers and _drafts. Prefer a plain directory pattern and a build step that writes only what should ship. You need all: when a framework's output uses _ names (SvelteKit's _app, Next.js's _next).

pitfalls.title: Assets outside the package directory
pitfalls.detail: //go:embed ../web/dist is an invalid pattern. Put a tiny package next to the assets (web/embed.go exporting an fs.FS) and import it.

pitfalls.title: Building before the frontend exists
pitfalls.detail: A pattern that matches nothing fails the build ("pattern dist: no matching files found", or "cannot embed directory dist: contains no embeddable files" for an empty directory). Build the frontend first in CI and in the Dockerfile.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting the directory prefix
pitfalls.detail: static.ReadFile("app.css") fails: the name is static/app.css. Use fs.Sub to serve a directory as the root.

quiz.q: //go:embed static is above an embed.FS. Which of static/app.css, static/_draft.html, static/.env end up in the binary?
quiz.why: Directory patterns skip names that start with . or _; the all: prefix would include them.

quiz.q: You edit a template file while the compiled server is running. When do users see the change?
options: After a rebuild and a restart
quiz.why: The compiler copied the file into the binary; the running program never reads the file on disk.

quiz.q: Why should newHandler take an fs.FS instead of an embed.FS?
options: embed.FS can't be passed to functions
So tests and development can pass fstest.MapFS or os.DirFS
quiz.why: Depending on the interface keeps the decision about where files come from in main.

body:
## Concept

`//go:embed pattern` above a package-level variable tells the compiler to read files from the
package directory (or below it) at build time and store them in the binary:

- `string` or `[]byte`: exactly one file, its content.
- `embed.FS`: any number of files and directories, as a read-only file system that
  implements `fs.FS`, `fs.ReadDirFS` and `fs.ReadFileFS`.

Patterns use `/` on every OS and may not contain `.`, `..` or a leading `/`. A directory
pattern takes the whole subtree except names beginning with `.` or `_`; `all:dir` takes
everything. The program never looks for those files at run time, so it works from any
working directory, in a `FROM scratch` container, or copied to another machine.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/C++: C23 (and C++26) add `#embed` for one file; before that, `xxd -i` or linker tricks.
  `embed.FS` adds the directory tree and a file-system API on top.
- Java: like resources on the classpath (`getResourceAsStream`), but there's no JAR or
  classloader: the files are bytes in the executable, and the API is the same `fs.FS` you'd
  use for a directory.
- Python: `importlib.resources` for package data, minus the packaging metadata you need to
  get the files into the wheel.
- Node: the closest is a bundler inlining assets, or Node's single executable applications
  (still experimental). In Go it's part of the plain `go build`.

## How it works

The `go` command finds the `//go:embed` lines, checks the patterns, and hands the matching
files to the compiler, which stores their contents in the binary's read-only data. An
`embed.FS` value is just a sorted list of names and contents, so `Open`, `ReadDir` and
`ReadFile` are lookups in memory. Its files report a zero modification time; `go list
-json` shows each package's `EmbedPatterns` and `EmbedFiles` if you want to see what was
matched.

## Design notes

Put embedded assets behind a small package that exports an `fs.FS` (for example a `web`
package next to the frontend's `dist/`), and make every consumer take `fs.FS`. Then `main`
chooses: the embedded files in production, `os.DirFS("web/dist")` behind a `-dev` flag for
live editing, `fstest.MapFS` in tests. Since embedded files have no modification time, give
built assets content-hashed names (Vite does this by default) and serve them with a long
`Cache-Control`, or add an `ETag` middleware; otherwise browsers have nothing to revalidate
against and download them again.

expected.embed-basics:
version: "1.4.2\n"
after rewriting version.txt on disk: "1.4.2\n"
//go:embed static
  static/app.css
  static/index.html
//go:embed all:static
  static/.env.local
  static/_draft.html
  static/app.css
  static/index.html
index.html starts with "<!doctype html>"
_draft.html not embedded: open static/_draft.html: file does not exist
expected.templates-server:
GET /hello/Ay%C5%9Fe 200

Hoş geldin, Ayşe!

GET /hello/%3Cscript%3E 200

Hoş geldin, <script>!

GET /static/app.css 200 body { font-family: system-ui; } GET /static/_draft.html 404 404 page not found GET /static/app.css 200 /* test */
